the following: (1) the strain pattern in a tectonically active zone undergoing unconfined transpressional deformation, (2) the partitioning of deformation between pre-existing faults and adjacent rocks, and (3) the development of folds in a transpressionally active area.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the strain pattern and/or the fold styles in transpression can be controlled by the angle of convergence, the ease of fault slip and the thickness and/or rigidity of the deformed layers.

strain pattern and fold styles are strongly controlled by the relative magnitude of the two components of transpressional deformation (simple shear and pure shear) and by the angle of convergence between the two boundary walls.

the spatial distribution of transpressive strain and fold styles in a transpressional tectonic zone depend strongly on the angle of convergence, the presence and/or absence of pre-existing faults, and the ease of slip along them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the strain pattern and the fold styles in a transpressional zone are controlled by the angle of convergence between the walls and by the partitioning of transpression along pre-existing fault zones.

strain patterns in transpressional zones depend on the relative magnitude of pure and simple shear components, which in turn are dependent on the angle of convergence between the two walls, the ease of fault slip, and the pre-existing fault zone.

strain partitioning between the pre-existing fault and the surrounding rocks, and/or the fold rotation in transpressional systems are strongly dependent upon the angle of convergence and the lubrication of the fault.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the initial angle between the ISAmax and the plane of simple shearing is a function of the angle of convergence and the magnitude of the transpressive strain.

the spatial and temporal evolution of strain and/or fold patterns in a partitioned transpressive zone can be understood by combining the concepts of finite strain analysis, strain partitioning and the kinematics of folding.

the initial strain patterns (elliptical strain markers and folds) and their subsequent evolution (decrease in the angle of the ISAmax, rotation of the folds) in a tectonically active zone depend on both the angle of convergence and the ease of slip on a pre-existing fault.
